entries.title: Tibetan at a glance
body: Tibetan is spoken by about six million people across the Tibetan Plateau and in exile communities in India, Nepal and beyond. It belongs to the Sino-Tibetan family. The main spoken varieties (Central or Lhasa, Amdo and Kham) differ a lot, but share one written language.

The verb comes last. The ending of a sentence shows whether you speak about yourself (ཡིན, ཡོད) or about others (རེད, ཡོད་རེད), and whether you saw something yourself (འདུག). Lhasa Tibetan is tonal, with a high and a low tone.

examples.r: Nga pöke lopjong che kyi yö.

entries.title: How Tibetan script works
body: The Tibetan script was created in the 7th century from an Indian Brahmi script. It has 30 consonant letters, each with an inherent a, and four vowel marks: ི (i), ུ (u), ེ (e) and ོ (o). The everyday printed style is called Uchen (དབུ་ཅན, “with a head”).
Words are not separated by spaces. Instead a small dot, the tsheg (་), follows every syllable, and a vertical stroke, the shad (།), ends a phrase or sentence.
Spelling is old and pronunciation has moved on. Letters can be stacked above and below the main letter, and many of them are silent: བཀྲ་ཤིས is said tashi, and བསྒྲུབས is said druk.

entries.title: Is, has, and their negatives
entries.body: Which word you use depends on who you are talking about, and how you know.

entries.title: Honorific words
entries.body: Tibetan has a set of respectful words used when speaking to or about others, especially elders and monks. Using them is a large part of being polite.

entries.title: Numbers and Tibetan digits
entries.body: Tibetan has its own digits. In counting from 21 upwards, a short linking syllable goes between tens and units: ཉི་ཤུ་རྩ་གཅིག (nyishu tsa chik) is 21.

entries.title: The khata
body: A khata (ཁ་བཏགས) is a white scarf, usually silk, offered as a sign of respect and good wishes: to welcome or say goodbye to a guest, at weddings and New Year, and when visiting a monastery or meeting a lama.
It is held out with both hands. When it is offered to a lama, people bow slightly, and the lama often places it back around their neck as a blessing.
